analysis.one_liner: Bans federal agencies from counting climate damage costs in energy and pollution rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on July 7, 2016 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Department of Energy and the EPA from using the "social cost of carbon" or "social cost of methane" — the government's dollar estimates of the damage each ton of those emissions does — in any cost-benefit analysis, rule, or guidance, unless Congress first passed a law explicitly allowing it. It would also require the EPA to report how many agency actions since January 2009 relied on those estimates. In practice, that would make it much harder to justify rules that limit carbon and methane pollution from coal, oil, and gas.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers, along with manufacturers and power plants facing EPA and DOE climate rules. Agency cost-benefit analyses rely on the social cost of carbon to show that emission limits produce benefits exceeding their costs; without that number, rules that raise the price of fossil energy become much harder to defend in court and in public. The bill's own findings say its purpose is to stop rules "regulating or prohibiting" coal and other fossil fuel use [S3]. The EPA reporting requirement would also hand opponents of climate regulation a catalog of rulemakings to target [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would ban the EPA and DOE from using the social cost of carbon or methane anywhere — in cost-benefit analyses required under Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, in rulemakings, in guidance, or as a justification for any action — unless Congress enacts a law explicitly authorizing it.

The bill's findings state that DOE and EPA rules justified by these estimates are aimed at fossil fuels, specifically coal, and would otherwise cost American families billions per year — so the ban is designed to blunt rules restricting coal mining and use and other fossil fuel production.

The social cost of methane definition in the bill points directly at EPA's September 2015 proposed and June 2016 final methane rules for the oil and gas sector, so the ban would undercut the accounting behind those specific rules.

It would require the EPA, within 120 days, to report every rulemaking, guidance document, and agency action since January 2009 that used either estimate, giving industry opponents a list of rules to challenge.

analysis.who_pays: The general public. The social cost of carbon exists so that agencies weigh the harms of climate change — storm damage, crop losses, health effects — against the costs of pollution limits. If agencies may not count those harms, rules that limit emissions look far more expensive relative to their benefits, and weaker rules or no rules result; the cost shows up as unchecked carbon and methane pollution rather than as a line item. Households and businesses would also bear any increases in climate-related damages that stronger rules would have avoided.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through unchecked climate pollution

drawbacks.text: Banning the metric entirely would leave agencies unable to weigh climate damages at all, even in updated form. The bill defines the prohibited social cost of carbon as 'any other estimate of the monetized damages associated with an incremental increase in carbon dioxide emissions,' so agencies could not substitute a revised methodology — the only escape is a new act of Congress.

Supporters' core objection — that the Obama-era estimates used global rather than domestic damages, omitted the discount rates OMB guidance requires, and were adopted without public notice and comment — is a fair critique of methodology, but those defects could have been fixed by revising the estimates rather than prohibiting agencies from monetizing carbon damages altogether.

Because the bill targets 'any action' by the Energy Secretary under any authority and the EPA under the Clean Air Act, it would reach beyond cost-benefit paperwork and constrain the legal and economic justification for existing and future emission standards, shifting those costs onto people exposed to pollution instead of the regulated industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill rests on a genuine grievance — the original 2009-2010 social cost of carbon estimates were developed by an interagency working group without formal notice-and-comment, used global damages, and departed from OMB's prescribed discount rates, as the bill's findings document [S3]. But the remedy is not calibration; it is prohibition. The bill would bar agencies from counting the cost of climate damage in any form, which does not make those damages disappear — it just makes them invisible when rules are weighed. The benefit flows to fossil fuel producers facing emission limits; the cost lands on the public as weaker pollution protection and a mandatory EPA report whose main use would be cataloging rules for future attacks. An honest supporter could have sought a corrected, domestic-only estimate with proper peer review; this bill instead removes the number altogether.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and died there, with no hearing, markup, or vote of any kind, before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Evan Jenkins of West Virginia introduced the bill on July 7, 2016, joined by original sponsors Womack, Culberson, LaHood, and Mullin, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Twenty-four Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

The full action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral — no subcommittee or committee action, no floor vote — and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without the bill moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, agencies retained the ability to count the damages of carbon and methane emissions when weighing pollution rules through the end of the Congress — so the public was spared a change that would have weakened the accounting behind climate and methane rules. Fossil fuel producers lost a chance to blunt those rules, though their broader effort continued in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people exposed to pollution; the bill died

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and none were Democrats; the bill never reached a floor or committee vote, so there is no roll call to break down.

industries.note: The bill's findings single out rules 'regulating or prohibiting' the mining and use of coal as justified by the social cost of carbon, and the sponsor represents West Virginia coal country. Blocking agencies from counting carbon damages would make the rules constraining coal harder to defend, preserving coal's market position at the public's expense.

The bill's definition of the social cost of methane is drawn verbatim from EPA's 2015-2016 methane rules for new and modified oil and gas sources. Banning the estimate would undercut the benefit side of the ledger for those rules and any successors, sparing producers the cost of methane controls.
DOE efficiency standards and rules that favor low-carbon energy are typically justified using the social cost of carbon; removing it would tilt future cost-benefit analyses against them.
